evidence_notes: Claim: the author did not support the claim that Venus is a worthy pursuit, because he dwells on danger rather than benefit. Support: three quoted passages from source paragraphs 2, 3 and 6 (corrosive sulfuric acid clouds, 800-degree temperatures, 90x atmospheric pressure), each followed by a brief gloss ('which gives the idea that it is a very dangerous place'). Connection to claim is stated but by restatement. ORG 4 (idea stated early and held, opening and closing present, all body material relates; rung 5 fails because the three quotes are interchangeable instances of the same point, sequenced by source-paragraph order, and the closing only restates the opening). DEV 4 (rung 4 yes: connection stated for the quotes; rung 5 fails because the glosses restate the quote rather than add interpretation, and the paragraph-6 quote is left to speak for itself; quotes are marked and sit alongside the writer's sentences rather than inside them). CONV 3 (rung 3 yes, nothing forces a guess; rung 4 fails because errors accumulate and force re-reading - 'This is even more if a danger sign', 'no one has went', 'many of times', 'tempetures', 'humas'). ARG 4 (rung 4 yes: one reason genuinely reasoned - the author's near-exclusive emphasis on hazards with no offsetting good is given as why the claim goes unsupported; rung 5 fails - no opposing reading acknowledged and answered, no qualification, no explicit governing principle, and the conclusion is what the prompt's framing implies).

Claim: driverless cars are a good idea but not yet safe, and liability for crashes falls to the manufacturer. Support: a realized hypothetical of a businessperson completing paperwork during the commute while a co-worker does not, and a liability scenario tied to a programming malfunction; no source material used. Connection stated for the commuting example ('all because you own a driverless car and can get more done'). ORG 3 (rung 4 fails: the controlling idea does not hold - it moves from 'not yet a safe one' to 'never going to be a legitimate guaranteed safety vehicle', the intro opens mid-argument on liability, and body unit 2 starts on the benefits and finishes on the crash/liability objection). DEV 4 (rung 4 yes: connection stated for the commuting example; rung 5 fails because support is not specific throughout - the con side is a chain of rhetorical questions with no realized case). CONV 3 (rung 3 yes, meaning recoverable; rung 4 fails - 'theres been a bit of an interfence with your work and didn't have time... on th ewy to work' and similar require re-reading, plus 'soembody', 'responibility', 'getg'). ARG 5 (rung 5 yes: the position is genuinely qualified where the issue warrants it - good in principle, unsafe in practice - the benefit side is acknowledged and answered by weighing damage costs against time saved, and the essay reaches a conclusion the keep-or-not framing does not imply, proposing restricted deployment for city tours or neighborhood speeds; rung 6 fails - no strongest objection answered and the prompt's terms are not reframed).

Claim: the facial-emotion computer system is valuable because it reads emotions, aids communication, and helps teachers. Support: Mona Lisa percentages (83% happy, 9% disgusted, 6% fearful, 2% angry), the 44 major muscles / 3D model process, and the zygomatic major vs risorius false-smile contrast - all lifted from the source with minimal transformation and stitched between short writer sentences. ORG 4 (rung 4 yes: three-reason thesis stated in the opening, three matching body units, closing present; rung 5 fails - the three reasons are interchangeable and the two closing paragraphs restate rather than build). DEV 3 (patchwriting cap: source phrasing reproduced with little transformation and lightly stitched - 'to an expert, faces don't lie these muscle cluses are sometimes used to spot when a smiling politican... isnt't being truthful' - which caps the trait at 3; not predominantly copied, so not 1). CONV 3 (rung 3 yes, meaning stays recoverable; rung 4 fails - errors accumulate heavily and force re-reading: run-ons fusing two source sentences without punctuation, 'This computer system software helped the Mona Lisa's emotions', 'weather' for whether, 'bielive', 'peolpe', 'compyter'). ARG 4 (rung 4 yes: the teacher reason is reasoned - the system detects boredom or confusion, which tells teachers the lesson needs review, so it helps them; rung 5 fails - no opposing view, no qualification, the explicit principle offered is borrowed source phrasing, and the essay circles back to its opening claim).

Largely a retelling of the source article; the writer's own claim - that NASA released the images to draw public attention to Mars and that this was 'what NASA wanted all along' - appears only in the final paragraph. Support: Viking 1 over Cydonia, the quoted NASA caption, the pop-icon spread over 25 years, Michael Malin's Mars Orbiter Camera image ten times sharper, Jim Garvin's Middle Butte comparison. ORG 3 (rung 4 fails: the controlling idea is weakly located - stated only in the conclusion while paragraphs 1-2 run as chronological narrative with no governing position; the opening is a date hook that does not orient, and the Hollywood-film/grocery-checkout stretch is a digression). DEV 4 (rung 4 yes: connection stated for some support - 'the authors used the photo as a propaganda to get the publics attention to Mars, and it rsulted on good high notes'; rung 5 fails because most of the specific material is reported narrative left unexplained, and some paraphrase is loose enough to distort the source - the snapshot 'sent to the sister ship Viking 2', the May 2001 date). CONV 3 (rung 3 yes, meaning recoverable throughout; rung 4 fails - 'the Martian came equivalent of a butte or mesa' and 'Although this one had an unsual shadows' force re-reading, alongside 'contrivsory', 'landfrom', 'rsulted', 'capition'). ARG 3 (rung 4 fails: reasoning is asserted, not shown - the essay narrates NASA's proof rather than saying why anything follows, and the closing inference from 'the public responded' to 'it was what NASA wanted all along' is asserted; the essay circles its position).

Claim: keep the Electoral College because it is more reliable and more accurate than election by popular vote. Support: the source-one definition of the process (paragraph 2), the precinct scenario showing that a voter is actually selecting the state's electors (paragraph 6), and a hypothetical woman voting for the better-looking candidate, offered to show why unfiltered popular voting is inaccurate. ORG 4 (rung 4 yes: thesis stated early, restated as each body topic sentence, opening and closing both present; rung 5 fails - the two reasons overlap heavily and could swap without loss). DEV 4 (rung 4 yes: connection stated for the looks-voting hypothetical - 'that isnt an ancurate vote cause she just voted for the president she likes'; rung 5 fails - support is not specific throughout, the claim that electors are 'carryfully selected' is asserted, and the stated connections collapse into 'so thats one of the reasons why we should keep the electoral college'; source material is cited but sits alongside the writer's sentences). CONV 3 (rung 3 yes: meaning stays recoverable with repair; rung 4 fails - errors accumulate and force re-reading, e.g. 'they are chose, not just how much the voters like them but their cababilities so more modern. Also more reliable.' and 'what if want to run this country into the ground', plus 'precint'/'pricent', 'carryfully', 'ancurate'). ARG 4 (rung 4 yes: one reason reasoned - voters choose on appearance and likability, electors are chosen for capability, so elector selection is the more accurate route; rung 5 fails - opposition is mentioned in the intro but never answered, no qualification, and the conclusion is exactly what the keep-or-abolish framing implies).

Claim: keep the Electoral College - a constitutional tradition whose benefits outweigh the objections. Support: Posner on disputed outcomes being less likely (2012 electoral vs popular percentages, winner-take-all magnifying slight pluralities), Plumer's Gallup poll showing over 60% preferring direct election, and Posner's trans-regional appeal argument quoted with paragraph citations. ORG 4 (rung 4 yes: thesis stated at the end of the intro and held, both frame slots do work, all three body units relate; rung 5 fails - the two pro-EC evidence units are independent supports that could swap without loss). DEV 4 (rung 4 yes: connection stated for each piece - 'this demostrates', 'that means that', 'that highlights how'; rung 5 fails because those explanations restate or drift into unrelated assertions about voting being made 'easy and comfortable' rather than interpreting the evidence, and the 2012 figures are misreported). CONV 3 (rung 3 yes overall; rung 4 fails - errors accumulate and force re-reading: 'This help people by making easily the hour of vote for a candidate', 'we have changing many things', 'comfortables', 'presindet', 'landsalide', 'demostrates'). ARG 4 (rung 4 yes: the trans-regional reason is reasoned - no region holds enough electoral votes, so a regional favorite gains nothing by running up margins where he already wins; rung 5 fails on the compound - the Plumer objection is acknowledged and given a thin answer ('yet that has happened very rarely'), but the conclusion is precisely what the keep-or-change framing implies).

Claim: schools should not invest in the Facial Action Coding System, for three reasons - distraction, cost, and student unwillingness to have emotions read. Support: an attributed 72% student-distraction figure, a list of better uses for school money (sporting equipment, food, building extension), and the Dr. Huang quote about a classroom computer recognizing confusion or boredom, turned against itself. ORG 4 (rung 4 yes: three-part thesis stated early and echoed in each topic sentence, opening and closing present, all body units relate; rung 5 fails - the three reasons are interchangeable, and two body units end on a sentence belonging to the next unit). DEV 4 (rung 4 yes: the Huang quote is followed by a stated connection - students find it embarrassing and discouraging for teachers to know how they feel; rung 5 fails - support is not specific throughout, the distraction paragraph is circular assertion, and the closing 62% figure does not bear on any claim). CONV 4 (rung 4 yes: errors are visible but do not accumulate - 'at least on technological device', 'the materials that is needed', 'harder to the teacher'; rung 5 fails because sentence shape is formulaic across the three body openings and 'Putting this Facial Action Coding System in all classroom can be schools go in debt' loses control). ARG 4 (rung 4 yes: the privacy reason is reasoned - students going through a rough time would find it discouraging to attend a class where teachers can read their feelings; rung 5 fails - the pro-side quote is repurposed rather than answered as an opposing position, no qualification, no explicit governing principle, and the conclusion is what the prompt's framing implies).

Claim: the president should be elected by popular vote because it is fairer and less complicated than the Electoral College. Support: three quoted Plumer passages - candidates ignoring states they cannot win, seventeen states unvisited in the 2000 campaign with 25 large media markets seeing no ad, and the tie scenario in which Wyoming's single representative for 500,000 voters equals California's 55 for 35 million - each followed by a stated inference. ORG 4 (rung 4 yes: two-reason thesis stated at the end of the intro and held, opening and closing present, both body units relate; rung 5 fails - fairness and simplicity are independent supports that could swap without loss, and the closing restates). DEV 4 (rung 4 yes: connection stated for each quote - 'that is not fair every state should be able to see the candidates'; rung 5 fails - support is not specific throughout, the claim that there is 'no way of cheating in the popular vote method' is unsupported assertion, and the tie-quote gloss just repeats the figures). CONV 4 (rung 4 yes: errors are occasional and meaning never needs repair - 'seventeeen', 'absoloutley', a dropped word in 'The popular is just fine'; rung 5 fails because run-ons such as 'That is not fair every state should be able to see the candidates' and 'The popular vote method is a lot more simple it doesn't require all of these steps' cost the reader a small repair, and the intro is choppily repetitive). ARG 4 (rung 4 yes: the swing-state reason is reasoned - candidates skip uncompetitive states, so those voters never see the candidates and cannot judge them, so the outcome is unfair; rung 5 fails on the compound - the principle that every citizen's vote should be their own is made explicit, but the conclusion is exactly what the popular-vote-or-Electoral-College framing implies, and no pro-EC argument is answered).

Claim: it would be a good idea for classroom technology to read students' emotional expressions. Support: the borrowed Web-ad example and the source's confusion/boredom detection, plus generalized assertions that students come home complaining about stress, bullying and homework, and the writer's own report of often not following the teacher. ORG 3 (rung 4 fails: the idea is stated but does not hold - one body unit is about persuading students to accept the technology rather than whether it is good, and the final unit digresses into a direct lecture telling students to put their phones down and read books, ending without closing). DEV 3 (rung 4 fails: the one specific borrowed example, the Web ad, is dropped and never connected; the rest is general gesture and the reader supplies the connections, with circular passages such as technology to read emotional expressions being 'the best idea in the world to read students emotional expressions, because some kids need it'). CONV 2 (rung 3 fails: at several points the reader must guess rather than repair - 'how you have time to get any of it done' reverses the intended meaning, 'parnters' is used for parents, 'Just think about how do you think teachers our school feel', 'when would not have as much problems' - alongside frequent run-ons and unresolved sentences). ARG 3 (rung 4 fails: reasoning is asserted, not shown - the essay repeatedly restates that the technology would be great and that teachers need to know how students feel, and later claims that cell phone use causes drama and that students should put devices away do not sit under the pro-technology position).

Claim: the Facial Action Coding System is a good idea because it could improve criminal investigation. Support: a realized hypothetical in which police, having arrested bank robbers, could photograph them and read their expressions with FACS instead of sitting down and working their way around to an interview; plus a borrowed quote about varying degrees of expression and an undeveloped aside about animation in television and video games. ORG 4 (rung 4 yes: the controlling idea opens the body and holds, the hook orients and the closing closes on the same two claims; rung 5 fails - the body unit does not build, the quote does not do the job it is attached to, and the animation sentence is tacked on). DEV 4 (rung 4 yes: the connection is stated - the photo-and-FACS route 'would make it easier on investigators' by contrast with the interview route; rung 5 fails - the animation claim has no support at all and the quote is left unexplained, so support is not specific and explained throughout). CONV 3 (rung 3 yes: meaning stays recoverable; rung 4 fails - errors accumulate and force re-reading, notably the long comma-spliced bank-robbery sentence, 'this is a gonna impact', the repeated 'the're' for they're/there, plus 'thier', 'artical', 'ivestigation', 'recgonizing' and uncapitalized sentence openings). ARG 4 (rung 4 yes: one reason reasoned - two investigative routes are set against each other and the essay says why the FACS route is preferable; rung 5 fails - no opposing consideration acknowledged or answered, no qualification, and no governing principle stated).
